master_narrator.agency_handoff_prompt:
The table was silent. Not the good, tired silence of a job well done. The sharp, brittle silence of sixteen people who had been breathing the same recycled air for too long.

Elias sat near the warmth of the firelight, carefully observing the exact friction coefficient of sixteen polymaths. The symptoms of the third-quarter isolation micro-stressors were manifesting rapidly across the room. It had been weeks of subterranean survival, of mitigating cortisol cascades and autonomic hypervigilance through their structured communal roast rituals and oxytocin vagal buffering. Yet tonight, the sanctuary's peace was teetering on the edge of collapse because Kaio had decided to filter the evening's soup stock through a sock. 

"It was a clean sock!" Kaio protested, his voice echoing too loudly off the high, vaulting walls of the cavern.

Elias watched the entire table nearly mutiny. The argument quickly fragmented along disciplinary lines—biology against logistics, safety versus discovery. He felt the familiar, heavy weight of his Taurus polarity inversion creeping in. Under extreme stress, the normally gentle philosopher and quiet observer in him dug his heels in with an immovable, deadpan stubbornness. He refused to intervene. He would sit here, perfectly still, until they realized the absurdity of their own noise.

The argument swirled around him, a desperate need for the crew to defend their respective boundaries and consume some shred of comfort in this quiet bioluminescent wonder. They were sixteen mugs raised in the warm circle of firelight while the captured geode hummed steadily beneath the floorboards, an ever-present reminder of their fragile existence. 'We brought eight centuries of differential calculus across the stars,' Elias thought to himself with a trace of dry amusement, 'yet here we sit arguing whether a sock belongs in the broth.'

He did not raise his voice or attempt to command the room. Instead, he simply waited, allowing his own stillness to attract the attention of those closest to him. It was a calculated risk. If you're complaining and no one is laughing, you're complaining wrong. Eventually, the sheer ridiculousness of the situation began to pierce through the tension. Someone snorted. Then another chuckled. 

Through the waning noise, Elias caught Elara's eye. Her warm, clinical gaze was tracking the exact same micro-cortisol baselines. Elias offered a small, imperceptible nod, signaling a subtle handoff. He would let this absurd tension completely play out until it shattered into cleansing hysteria, and then he would let Elara guide them all back to center. They would survive this night, as they always did, as long as they could continue to conceal their deeper existential dread behind a veil of dry, affectionate banter.
